title: Building Bridges
statement:
A river has a north bank and a south bank. Cities on the north bank are numbered by their position along the bank, and so are the cities on the south bank. You are given `n` candidate bridges; candidate `i` would join north city `a[i]` to south city `b[i]`.

Two chosen bridges **cross** if their order along the north bank is the opposite of their order along the south bank. Formally, bridges `(a1, b1)` and `(a2, b2)` cross when `a1 < a2` and `b1 > b2`, or `a1 > a2` and `b1 < b2`. Bridges that share a north city or share a south city (or are identical) do not cross, and a candidate may appear several times in the list, each copy being a separate bridge.

Choose as many bridges as possible so that no two chosen bridges cross, and print how many you can choose.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines contains two integers `a[i]` and `b[i]`.
outputFormat: Print one integer: the maximum number of pairwise non-crossing bridges.

examples.explanation: Sorted by north city the south cities are 5, 6, 3, 2. The best non-decreasing run is 5, 6 (bridges (1,5) and (2,6)), length 2. Any three bridges contain a crossing.
All bridges go straight across, so none of them cross.
The three bridges leaving north city 3 share an endpoint, so they never cross each other. Bridge (2,9) crosses all of them, so the answer is 3.

hints: Two bridges cross only when the order of their north cities disagrees with the order of their south cities. Sort the bridges by north city to fix one of the two orders.
After sorting by (north, south), a set of bridges is non-crossing exactly when their south cities never decrease along the sorted order.
So the answer is the length of the longest non-decreasing subsequence of the south cities; compute it in O(n log n) with binary search over tails.
